name: Vasavi
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Watters, Stephen. 2013. A Sociolinguistic Profile of the Bhils of Northern Dhule District. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2013-004. Dallas: SIL International. vi+125 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic survey (lexical similarity, intelligibility, bilingualism); Appendix C gives 210-item IPA wordlists for four Vasave villages (Kelpada, Dhanoura, Digiamba, Amoda) plus Bhilori, Noiri, Pauri and Nahali, with no stress marks (0 occurrences of IPA stress mark in the text). Confirms identity: 'What Grierson refers to as Dehwali is probably known to the researcher as Vasave' (section 1.2.1, citing LSI IX.iii:158).

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. 1907. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. IX Part III: Indo-Aryan Family, Central Group: The Bhil Languages, including Khandesi, Banjari or Labhani, Bahrupia, &c. Calcutta: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing. Section 'Dehawali', pp. 158-159 (pp. 171-172 of the DLI scan;ernet.dli.2015.61830).
sources.note: Nothing. The 'Pronunciation' paragraph on p. 158 (page scan viewed) notes only 'the drawling pronunciation of final vowels and the free use of the Anunasika', treatment of short a, dropping of initial h, deaspiration, s > h, loss of intervocalic r, and the cerebral l; no word about accent or stress. The only accent remark in the volume is the generic transliteration note ('When it is necessary to mark an accented syllable, the acute accent is used'), not applied to Dehawali.

sources.citation: Vasava, Jitendra V. Dehvali bhilo ni maukhik kathaono ane sanskrutik ane sahityik abyas. PhD thesis (Gujarati). Shodhganga handle 10603/540206.
sources.note: Gujarati folklore thesis on the Dehwali Bhils; Indian folklore theses sometimes open with a 'boli' (dialect) chapter listing sounds. Bitstreams were not downloadable at search time (HTTP 302).

sources.note: First-hand dialect field notes (12 pp.) by a trained Gujarati linguist on the Bhili of the Vasavi area; such LSBG field reports give phonetic and morphological observations; a central Indo-Aryan Bhil variety is expected to be described without lexical tone, but no tone or accent statement has been verified.
